text.en: In school Asha attended a health talk. "Healthy habits protect us from harm," said the counsellor.

Health includes physical, mental and social well-being. Children have a right to safety. Physical or emotional harm, sexual abuse, neglect and exploitation are forms of maltreatment. A child who feels unsafe can tell a trusted adult. Adults are responsible for helping the child get support.
Tobacco smoke and alcohol can harm health. Substance use problems can lead to dependence, and recovery may involve healthcare, counselling and social support.
This chapter distinguishes infectious and noncommunicable diseases and introduces diabetes, heart disease, cancer and HIV. Healthy habits, appropriate healthcare and safe environments can support well-being.
Health means being well in body, mind and society.

text.en: Child abuse can involve physical or emotional harm, sexual abuse, neglect, or exploitation. If someone makes a child feel unsafe, the child can tell a trusted adult. Responsibility for the harm belongs to the person causing it.

board.text: abuse

text.en: Substance misuse includes using medicines other than as directed or using alcohol or tobacco in ways that cause harm. People affected by substance use problems deserve support.

board.text: drug dependence

text.en: Substance misuse can affect health and behaviour and can lead to dependence. The effects vary with the substance and the circumstances.

board.text: tobacco hazards

text.en: Tobacco smoking causes lung disease and cancer.

board.text: alcohol harm

text.en: Alcohol harms the liver and the brain.

board.text: rehabilitation

text.en: De-addiction and rehabilitation measures with medical help and family support help people recover.

text.en: The chapter also lists common diseases and their prevention, and stresses healthy habits like clean food, exercise and avoiding addictive substances.

board.text: abuse

text.en: Physical health concerns the body. Mental health concerns thoughts, emotions and coping, while social well-being includes supportive relationships.

board.text: Health has physical, mental and social aspects

text.en: A person can need emotional or social support even when no physical disease has been found. Health is broader than the absence of illness.

board.text: Illness is only one part of health

text.en: Child maltreatment can involve physical injury, threats or humiliation, sexual abuse, or neglect of essential care.

board.text: Harm can take different forms

text.en: A child can speak up if someone ignores their boundaries or asks them to keep an unsafe secret. They can ask for help without having to prove what happened.

board.text: Personal boundaries matter

text.en: A parent, teacher, counsellor or another reliable adult can listen and help arrange support. Choose someone you feel safe telling.

board.text: Find a trusted adult

text.en: If the first adult does not listen or the situation remains unsafe, tell another trusted adult. Children do not have to solve the situation on their own.

board.text: Tell another adult if help does not follow

text.en: Listen when a friend says they feel unsafe. Avoid blaming them or passing their story around. Help them reach a trusted adult who can act.

board.text: Respond to a friend with care

text.en: A medicine meant for one person may be unsuitable for someone else. Ask a trusted adult or healthcare professional if you are unsure about a medicine.

board.text: Use medicines only as directed

text.en: A person may continue using a substance even when it is causing problems. It helps to recognise dependence as a health issue and seek support.

board.text: Dependence can make stopping difficult

text.en: Smoking increases the risk of lung disease, heart disease and some cancers. Smoke can also affect people nearby.

board.text: Tobacco smoke increases disease risk

text.en: Alcohol can change how the brain works before its longer-term effects appear. Repeated harmful use can also damage the liver and other organs.

board.text: Alcohol can affect judgement and coordination

text.en: Healthcare, counselling and support from trusted people can help someone recover. Setbacks do not mean that recovery is impossible.

board.text: Recovery often takes time and support

text.en: An infectious disease begins with an infectious agent. The right prevention measures depend on which disease is involved.

board.text: An infectious disease can be caused by a pathogen

text.en: Diabetes and most heart disease are noncommunicable. Several factors, including inherited traits and the environment, can influence risk.

board.text: Noncommunicable diseases do not pass between people

text.en: Insulin helps control blood glucose. Diabetes can involve too little insulin, reduced response to it, or both.

board.text: Diabetes affects blood-glucose regulation

text.en: One factor can raise the chance of a disease without proving that someone has it. A health professional can assess findings and explain what they mean.

board.text: Risk is not the same as a diagnosis

text.en: Cardiovascular diseases affect the heart or blood vessels. Many factors influence risk, including smoking, high blood pressure and family history.

board.text: Heart and blood vessels work together

text.en: In cancer, some cells grow in an uncontrolled way and can damage nearby tissues. Different types have different causes and treatments.

board.text: Cancer is a group of diseases

text.en: HIV is a virus that affects immune cells. AIDS is a term for an advanced stage of HIV infection that effective care can help prevent.

board.text: HIV and AIDS describe different things

text.en: Sitting next to a classmate, sharing a meal or shaking hands does not spread HIV. Accurate information helps reduce unfair treatment.

board.text: Ordinary classroom contact does not transmit HIV

text.en: Sleep, movement, varied meals and supportive relationships can help the body and mind. They improve well-being without guaranteeing that every illness can be prevented.

board.text: Healthy routines support several parts of health

text.en: Look for dependable health information and ask a trusted adult when something seems worrying. Health lessons explain concepts, while healthcare professionals assess individual concerns.

board.text: Health literacy includes knowing where to ask

problem.en: Whom can a child tell if someone makes them feel unsafe?

text.en: Children need trusted adults.
A parent, a teacher or a helpline can help.
So tell a trusted adult at once.

problem.en: A classmate says someone is ignoring their boundaries and asks them to keep it secret. What is a supportive response?

text.en: Listen and take their concern seriously.

why.en: They do not have to prove what happened to ask for help.

text.en: Help them reach a trusted adult, such as a teacher or counsellor.

why.en: Adults can take responsibility for arranging appropriate help.

problem.en: Can diabetes be passed to a classmate by sitting nearby?

text.en: Diabetes is a noncommunicable disease.

why.en: It involves regulation of blood glucose.

text.en: Sitting together does not pass it between people.

why.en: Distinguish disease risk factors from infection.

problem.en: A student worries they could get HIV by sharing a desk. How would you respond?

text.en: Ordinary school contact does not spread HIV.

why.en: Sharing a desk is ordinary day-to-day contact.

text.en: Continue to treat the classmate with respect.

why.en: Health facts can prevent unnecessary exclusion.

prompt.en: A friend says Smoking is harmless in small amounts. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Tobacco harms the lungs and heart.

points.en: Health covers body, mind and society.
Tell a trusted adult if unsafe.
Tobacco and alcohol harm the body.
